content: Densa Densa is a fictional parody organization modeled after Mensa International. The name Densa is a humorous play on the words Mensa and dense, implying a society for individuals with exceptionally low IQs, in contrast to Mensa, which is for those with exceptionally high IQs. The term is typically used in a comedic or satirical context. For instance, someone might jokingly suggest that a Mensa member belongs in Densa after doing something foolish. This concept is almost always employed in a lighthearted manner, often accompanied by a playful tone. The idea of an organization for the intellectually dense first appeared in the Boston & Outskirts Mensa Bulletin (BOMB) in August 1974, in a puzzle titled A-Bomb-inable Puzzle II by John D. Coons. This puzzle referenced The Boston chapter of Densa, the low IQ society. Subsequent issues of the bulletin included additional puzzles and jokes about the group, which were widely reprinted by other Mensa group bulletins. Over time, the concept of a low IQ society gained broader recognition during the 1970s, with others creating quizzes and similar humorous content. In 1983, a humor book titled The Densa Quiz: The Official & Complete DQ Test of the International Densa Society was authored by Stephen Price and J. Webster Shields. The concept of Densa continued to be referenced in various forms of media, including a mention in a 1987 article by William McGowan in The New York Times, titled A Sense of Belonging. While this article is not available through the New York Times archival service, it can be accessed via ProQuest.
